The Indian ilisha, Ilisha melastoma, exhibits life-history traits generally consistent with those of small, short-lived clupeiform fishes inhabiting warm coastal and estuarine waters. Field studies conducted at a stable water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C] have provided estimates for several key reproductive and developmental parameters. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) for reproductively active females averaged 4% [GSI = 4%] at a water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. In terms of body size, analyses of growth curves derived from length-frequency data indicate that the ultimate standard length, or asymptotic size, is approximately 14 centimeters [Li = approximately 14 centimeters], although some records from commercial catches suggest individuals can occasionally exceed this figure. This moderate maximum dimension is accompanied by a standard length at the onset of puberty of 6.5 centimeters [Lp = 6.5 centimeters], marking the point at which individuals transition to reproductive competence within this thermally stable environment.

Reproductive output and the mass of early life stages provide further insight into the species' demographic strategy. The dry weight of a newly emerged, yolk-sac-dependent larva, calculated from the mean egg diameter of approximately 1.46 millimeters, is estimated at 0.0016 grams [Wwb = 0.0016 grams]. This extremely small initial mass reflects the high fecundity typical of pelagic spawners that produce large numbers of small offspring. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum adult body mass predicted from the length-weight relationship, is approximately 48.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 48.8 grams], whereas the wet weight at around 4.7 grams [Wwp = around 4.7 grams] is attained at puberty. This substantial increase in body mass between the onset of maturity and the attainment of asymptotic size implies that a significant portion of somatic growth continues well after reproductive activity has commenced, a pattern observed in many iteroparous clupeids.

The chronological scale of the life cycle is tightly coupled to the warm thermal regime. At the prevailing water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C], the interval between fertilization and the hatching of the free-swimming larva is approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days]. This brief embryonic period, comparable to that documented for the European anchovy Engraulis encrasicolus under similar thermal conditions, allows for rapid turnover of generations in the productive coastal ecosystem. The duration from hatching to the completion of the lifespan is also constrained by temperature; maximum documented longevity in wild populations is approximately 365 days [am = approximately 365 days] at a temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. This annual cycle means that most individuals complete their entire life history within a single year, making Ilisha melastoma a relatively short-lived species even by clupeiform standards.

Comparisons with other members of the Pristigasteridae family highlight the relatively fast life-history pace of this species. Many larger clupeiform fishes attain lifespans of several years, yet the maximum longevity of 365 days [am = 365 days] recorded for Ilisha melastoma at 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C] places it firmly among the shorter-lived members of its lineage. The modest ultimate standard length of 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters] corresponds to a body size that is well below the maximum of around 22 centimeters sometimes reported in taxonomic accounts, possibly reflecting population-level variation in growth conditions or selective pressures from fishing. The wet weight at puberty of 4.7 grams [Wwp = 4.7 grams] is reached at a standard length of 6.5 centimeters [Lp = 6.5 centimeters], and this relatively early maturation relative to ultimate size supports the interpretation of a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive assurance over extended somatic investment.

Physiologically, the reproductive allocation appears modest when expressed as a proportion of body mass. The gonadosomatic index was 4% [GSI = 4%] during the spawning season at a temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. This low relative investment may be offset by a high spawning frequency, although direct estimates of batch fecundity remain limited for this species. The dry weight at birth of 0.0016 grams [Wwb = 0.0016 grams] for a newly hatched larva, combined with an incubation period of only 6 days [ab = 6 days] at 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C], underscores a strategy of producing many small, rapidly developing offspring. The ultimate wet weight of 48.8 grams [Wwi = 48.8 grams] represents the upper bound of somatic mass, and the modest size at maturity relative to this maximum suggests that energy is directed toward reproduction shortly after the minimal size for gonadal activation is attained.
